claims.text: As-deposited nanoscale FeMnNiGeSi-type films or nanoribbons have significant interface-induced stress.
These as-deposited materials have high defect densities and unrelaxed grain boundaries resulting from deposition.
Interfacial and surface stress-induced disorder and defects suppress the bulk-like magnetostructural transition in low-dimensional FeMnNiGeSi-type alloys.
Suppression of the bulk-like magnetostructural transition governs the low-field magnetocaloric response.
Interfacial stress and structural defects cause enhanced magnetic hysteresis during low-field cooling cycles.
Controlled post-deposition annealing can relieve interface-induced stress and reduce defect density.
Stress relaxation and defect reduction enable a magnetostructural transition that more closely resembles bulk behavior.
A more bulk-like magnetostructural transition reduces magnetic hysteresis.
A more bulk-like magnetostructural transition enhances the magnetocaloric effect.
Higher stress and defect concentrations broaden the transition.
Higher stress and defect concentrations increase hysteresis.
Annealed samples will exhibit lower magnetic hysteresis than the as-deposited baseline during low-field cooling cycles.
Annealed samples will exhibit a larger magnetocaloric temperature change than the as-deposited baseline during low-field cooling cycles.
The as-deposited baseline has a suppressed magnetocaloric response and significant hysteresis because of interface-induced stress and persistent defects.
Surface and interface effects dominate in FeMnNiGeSi-type films thinner than 100 nm.
Heat-transfer rate influences phase-transition dynamics at the specified cooling-cycle frequencies.
